abstract: Plant-associated microbial communities can improve plant resilience to stress and as such are a promising avenue for the future of agricultural technologies to improve crop health. Ideally, synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) are simplified versions of real-world communities that can recapitulate their function. However, SynCom applications often have variable results, we hypothesize is due to the gap between the ideal and realized community. Understanding the mechanisms that support effective SynCom assembly is a key step to unlocking this resource. We investigated how fungal assembly mechanisms (priority, diversity) impacted wheat response to drought. The SynComs contained a single pioneer fungus applied first, followed by low diversity (3 fungi) or high diversity (9 fungi) community inoculations. Plants were then grown under drought or well-watered conditions. We measured plant phenotypic traits and realized fungal community. Realized communities contained a small set of the inoculated SynCom taxa and were not impacted by any treatment. To understand this outcome, we asked if fungal traits or field distributions could predict fungal persistence. We found that persistent SynCom taxa were those that were highly connected hubs in the field network, suggesting that fungi that cooccur and interact with many taxa are more likely to succeed in SynCom applications. Initial and realized SynCom composition influenced plant performance but not in a systematic way. This study highlights the importance of considering natural microbial communities during SynCom design to increase establishment and success of fungal taxa to improve crop stress tolerance.
